Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

please make the prompt complete and easy to hand to someone preparing the rota include the location alder creek community garden and the fact that this is the teaching greenhouse do not include an invented year or a date for the week since neither has been decided keep the recipient instruction clear near the beginning and repeat it only where needed to prevent the printed copy from being sent to the wrong person the final request should retain the two section cues and the named plants volunteers and equipment do not add a summary after the request or write the rota itself", "output": "I need a clear prompt for a weekly watering rota for the teaching greenhouse at Alder Creek Community Garden. The rota should cover Monday through Sunday and show who checks each growing area and when they should water. I want the request to make clear that the person receiving the finished rota is Emmett, not Soraya. The greenhouse has six areas called the north seedling shelves, the east tomato beds, the west herb bench, the central propagation table, the hanging baskets by the south doors, and the small citrus corner near the sink. Use those names as written so volunteers can match the rota to the signs already in the greenhouse.

Please ask for a rota that can be printed on one page in portrait orientation, with a short plain-language note at the top about checking soil before adding water. The note should explain that a finger test is enough for ordinary pots and that trays of new seedlings need a closer look because their surface dries quickly. Ask for each day to have a morning check and an afternoon check, but do not imply that every area needs water at both times. The schedule should distinguish between looking at a plant and actually watering it so a volunteer does not treat every check as an instruction to soak the soil. Include a place to mark a completed check and a separate place to mark watering.

There are four regular volunteers, and the request should use their names in the rota. The volunteers are Lena Ortiz, who usually opens the greenhouse on Monday and Wednesday; Ravi Shah, who handles the tomato beds most often; June Park, who prefers afternoon work; and Emmett Vale, who can cover Saturday mornings. The rota should spread the work fairly across the week and avoid assigning anyone two areas at the same time. Make sure Emmett Vale is named as the recipient because he is collecting the printed copy on Friday, and keep Soraya Bell out of the recipient line. Soraya can appear only as the person who left a note about the broken hose near the south doors. The request should not assume that the hose has been repaired.

The practical details matter for the watering instructions. The tomatoes have drip lines that run from a timer, and volunteers should inspect the emitters rather than hand-watering the beds unless an emitter is visibly blocked. The herbs are in shallow pots and may need a small amount of water after a warm afternoon. The seedling trays are on capillary mats and should be checked for contact with the mat before anyone fills them. The citrus corner has one lemon tree and two young calamondins, and the citrus pots should not be left standing in water. Mention these details only where they help explain what a check means, and do not turn them into a general claim that every plant has the same needs.

The weather note for this particular week says Monday and Tuesday are expected to be cloudy with cool nights, Wednesday may reach twenty-six degrees Celsius, and Thursday is forecast to be breezy with a chance of light rain. Friday through Sunday have no reliable forecast yet. Ask the prompt to leave room for a brief daily weather note instead of treating this forecast as certain. The rain barrel is half full, and the tap beside the potting bench has a slow leak. Volunteers can use the blue watering cans from the rack but should return them there after use. The only watering wand with a working shutoff is marked green, so the request should not suggest that a different wand is available.

Section one should ask for the weekly schedule itself, with days in calendar order and the two check times visible for every day. Include a compact key for check only, water if needed, and task completed, and leave enough space for initials beside each mark. The rota should make clear that a missed morning check is not automatically permission to double the next watering. Say that a volunteer should tell the greenhouse coordinator if a scheduled check cannot be covered rather than silently moving another person's assignment. Ask for the schedule to fit the named areas and the four volunteers without creating a new role or inventing extra staff.

Section two should ask for a short notes area beneath the schedule, with room to record a dry tray, an obstructed drip emitter, a low barrel, or another condition that changes the next check. Give one ordinary example of a useful note without presenting it as a real event for this week. The example can say that a volunteer saw a dry seedling tray on Tuesday afternoon and told the coordinator. Keep that example separate from the actual forecast and from the note about the broken hose. Ask for the prompt to keep the wording practical and readable for volunteers who have not worked in this greenhouse before, but do not explain basic gardening at length.

The finished rota should not promise that any plant will thrive or that the weather will cooperate. It should not prescribe a fixed volume of water for every area, and it should not add chemical treatments or fertilizer instructions. The request should keep the schedule flexible enough for the soil check to matter while still giving volunteers a dependable weekly plan. Include the greenhouse coordinator as the person to contact when a plant looks unusual, but leave a blank for the coordinator's name and contact details because those have not been supplied. Ask for a simple, accessible layout with strong contrast and no reliance on color alone to distinguish a check from watering.

Please make the prompt complete and easy to hand to someone preparing the rota. Include the location Alder Creek Community Garden and the fact that this is the teaching greenhouse. Do not include an invented year or a date for the week since neither has been decided. Keep the recipient instruction clear near the beginning and repeat it only where needed to prevent the printed copy from being sent to the wrong person. The final request should retain the two section cues and the named plants, volunteers, and equipment. Do not add a summary after the request or write the rota itself."}]
